A Gradient Recovery Method for Electron Magnetohydrodynamics with Fractional Dissipation

Hailong Guo ††thanks: Chongqing Research Institute of Big Data, Peking University, Chongqing, 401332, China and School of Mathematics and Statistics, The University of Melbourne, Parkville, VIC 3010, Australia. hailong.guo@cqbdri.pku.edu.cn, hailong.guo@unimelb.edu.au    Ruimeng Hu ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, Department of Statistics and Applied Probability, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA 93106, USA. rhu@ucsb.edu    Qirui Peng ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA 93106, USA. qpeng9@ucsb.edu    Xu Yang ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, University of California, Santa Barbara, CA 93106, USA. xy6@ucsb.edu
Abstract

We propose and analyze a structure-preserving numerical method for the 2⁤122\tfrac{1}{2}-dimensional (2.5D) electron magnetohydrodynamics system with fractional dissipation on the periodic torus. The method works directly with the magnetic field components and combines this component formulation with the gradient recovery operator of [T. Chu, H. Guo, and Z. Zhang, SIAM J. Numer. Anal., 63 (2025), pp. 23–53]. We establish discrete energy stability for a semi-implicit structure-preserving formulation and use an explicit-Hall integrating-factor implementation for efficient computation on periodic grids. The fractional dissipation is treated exactly in Fourier space, and the in-plane divergence constraint is enforced by a spectral Hodge projection. Numerical experiments demonstrate second-order spatial convergence and stable Hall-driven dynamics across several benchmark tests.

keywords
Electron magnetohydrodynamics, gradient recovery, fractional Laplacian, structure preserving, energy stability.
††runningheads: A gradient recovery method for EMHD / H. Guo, R. Hu, Q. Peng, and X. Yang
MSC
65M60, 65M12, 76W05, 76E25.

1 Introduction

The electron magnetohydrodynamics (EMHD) system

∂t𝑩+∇×((∇×𝑩)×𝑩)=ν​Δ​𝑩,∇⋅𝑩=0,\partial_{t}\bm{B}+\nabla\times\!\bigl((\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}\bigr)=\nu\Delta\bm{B},\qquad\nabla\cdot\bm{B}=0, (1)

describes the evolution of a magnetic field 𝑩\bm{B} in a plasma regime where electron motion dominates and ions provide a neutralizing background. The model is widely used to study rapid magnetic reconnection and electron-scale magnetic dynamics in space and laboratory plasmas. In particular, the Hall effect allows electron motion to decouple from ion motion below the ion inertial length, leading to reconnection rates that can become largely independent of resistivity [13, 2, 29, 27].

The nonlinear Hall term ∇×((∇×𝑩)×𝑩)\nabla\times((\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}) in (1) contains one more spatial derivative than the nonlinear terms in standard MHD. This higher-order structure underlies many distinctive features of EMHD and makes the model considerably more challenging to analyze and discretize. On the physics side, the Hall term supports dispersive whistler waves, promotes open X-point structures in reconnection regions, and can generate elongated current sheets depending on the dominant dissipation mechanism [3, 25, 11]. On the mathematical side, the non-resistive system remains poorly understood: local well-posedness in general settings is open, while recent works have shown ill-posedness mechanisms and well-posedness results under special structures or partial dissipation [6, 22, 23].

The 2.52.5D setting and its physical relevance. We focus on the 2⁤122\tfrac{1}{2}-dimensional (2.52.5D) setting, in which the magnetic field has three components (Bx,By,Bz)(B_{x},B_{y},B_{z}) but depends only on the two spatial variables (x,y)(x,y). This is the minimal nontrivial geometry for EMHD: it retains the essential Hall coupling between the in-plane field and the out-of-plane component while avoiding the full complexity of a fully three-dimensional computation. In particular, it preserves current-sheet and magnetic-island structures arising in reconnection problems [25, 3, 12, 1]. This reduction is therefore not merely a simplifying assumption: the Hall term still retains the derivative structure responsible for the main analytical and numerical difficulties, while the computational cost remains far below that of a fully three-dimensional simulation. Moreover, the fractional-dissipation model studied here lies in a regime where available well-posedness theory applies [4]. Thus the 2.52.5D system provides a natural testbed for the structure-preserving scheme developed below.

Component formulation. Rather than using scalar flux-function variables, we formulate the method directly in terms of the magnetic field components (Bx,By,Bz)(B_{x},B_{y},B_{z}). Under the 2.5D assumption, the curl is ∇×𝑩=(∂yBz,−∂xBz,J)\nabla\times\bm{B}=(\partial_{y}B_{z},\,-\partial_{x}B_{z},\,J) with J=∂xBy−∂yBxJ=\partial_{x}B_{y}-\partial_{y}B_{x} the out-of-plane current. Expanding the Hall term component by component yields the closed system

∂tBx+∂y(𝑩⋅∇Bz)+Λα​Bx\displaystyle\partial_{t}B_{x}+\partial_{y}(\bm{B}\cdot\nabla B_{z})+\Lambda^{\alpha}B_{x} =0,\displaystyle=0, (2a)
∂tBy−∂x(𝑩⋅∇Bz)+Λα​By\displaystyle\partial_{t}B_{y}-\partial_{x}(\bm{B}\cdot\nabla B_{z})+\Lambda^{\alpha}B_{y} =0,\displaystyle=0, (2b)
∂tBz+𝑩⋅∇J+Λα​Bz\displaystyle\partial_{t}B_{z}+\bm{B}\cdot\nabla J+\Lambda^{\alpha}B_{z} =0,\displaystyle=0, (2c)

with ∇⋅𝑩=0\nabla\cdot\bm{B}=0, where Λα=(−Δ)α/2\Lambda^{\alpha}=(-\Delta)^{\alpha/2} is the fractional Laplacian with α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2]. This is the system discretized in the rest of the paper.

The in-plane pair (Bx,By)(B_{x},B_{y}) is driven by gradients of BzB_{z}; the out-of-plane component BzB_{z} is advected by the in-plane current JJ. Local well-posedness of (2) follows from Chae–Wan–Wu [4], whose analysis requires fractional dissipation of order α>1\alpha>1;11 1 In our convention Λα=(−Δ)α/2\Lambda^{\alpha}=(-\Delta)^{\alpha/2}, equivalently (−Δ)β(-\Delta)^{\beta} with β>1/2\beta>1/2. our range α∈(1,2]\alpha\in(1,2] lies in this regime.

Relation to the scalar formulation. The same 2.5D dynamics can also be written in scalar variables by setting 𝑩=∇×(a​𝒆z)+b​𝒆z\bm{B}=\nabla\times(a\bm{e}_{z})+b\bm{e}_{z}, where aa is the flux function (Bx=∂yaB_{x}=\partial_{y}a, By=−∂xaB_{y}=-\partial_{x}a) and b=Bzb=B_{z}, giving

∂ta+ay​bx−ax​by\displaystyle\partial_{t}a+a_{y}b_{x}-a_{x}b_{y} =μ​Δ​a,\displaystyle=\mu\Delta a, (3a)
∂tb−ay​Δ​ax+ax​Δ​ay\displaystyle\partial_{t}b-a_{y}\Delta a_{x}+a_{x}\Delta a_{y} =ν​Δ​b,\displaystyle=\nu\Delta b, (3b)

with current J=−Δ​aJ=-\Delta a and resistivities μ,ν≥0\mu,\nu\geq 0. This form is convenient for PDE analysis, since the in-plane divergence constraint is built in and the Hall cancellation that underpins energy estimates is transparent. Local well-posedness under partial resistivity (μ>0\mu>0 or ν>0\nu>0) is due to Dai–Babaei [6, 7]; see [8, 9, 10, 22, 23, 24, 20, 21] for the broader literature. For low-order finite element discretization, however, (3) is less convenient than the component formulation: the Hall term in (3b) is third order in the flux function, through ax​Δ​ay−ay​Δ​ax=𝑩x​y⋅∇Ja_{x}\Delta a_{y}-a_{y}\Delta a_{x}=\bm{B}_{xy}\cdot\nabla J. This leads to a parabolic time-step restriction τ≲h2/|∇a|\tau\lesssim h^{2}/|\nabla a|, far more severe than the hyperbolic τ≲h/|𝑩|\tau\lesssim h/|\bm{B}| associated with the component system, and compounds the error of approximating JhJ_{h} and then differentiating it again. In (2), by contrast, JhJ_{h} is computed directly from first derivatives of (Bx,h,By,h)(B_{x,h},B_{y,h}), and the remaining Hall structure involves only second-order discrete operators. These considerations motivate our choice of the component formulation (2) as the primary computational representation.

Gradient recovery methods. Gradient recovery is a classical post-processing technique in finite element analysis: from a C0C^{0} finite element solution, whose gradient is generally discontinuous across element interfaces, one reconstructs a smoother and often superconvergent gradient. Two classical constructions are the superconvergent patch recovery (SPR) [32] and the polynomial-preserving recovery (PPR) [31]; recovered gradients also yield asymptotically exact a posteriori error estimators [26]. Recovery techniques have further been used in C0C^{0} linear discretizations of fourth-order problems [19], high-frequency wave propagation [16], elliptic interface problems [17, 15, 18], and the spectral computation of topological edge modes in photonic graphene [14]. In the present work, we employ the recovery operator [5] for a different purpose: not as an error estimator, but as a constructive device that makes the second-order discrete Hall operators computable on C0C^{0} linear elements, for which the required second derivatives are otherwise unavailable.

Numerical approach and contributions. The key insight is that the component formulation (2) reduces the Hall derivative count from three to two, and the gradient recovery operator GhG_{h} of Chu, Guo, and Zhang [5] then provides an accurate and stable way to approximate the remaining second-order Hall structure using C0C^{0} linear elements. A semi-implicit treatment of the Hall term with an exact integrating-factor method for the fractional Laplacian gives unconditional diffusion stability, leaving only the hyperbolic CFL τ≲h/|𝑩|\tau\lesssim h/|\bm{B}| from the explicit Hall evaluation.

The present work combines the 2.5D component formulation with the gradient recovery framework [5], leading to a practical discretization based on C0C^{0} linear elements and an efficient Fourier realization on periodic grids. For the analysis, we introduce a semi-implicit structure-preserving formulation and establish discrete energy stability estimates. Numerical experiments demonstrate second-order spatial convergence and illustrate stable Hall-driven dynamics across several benchmark problems.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. Section 2 presents the spatial discretization, the recovery gradient operator, the discrete Hall nonlinearities, and the time discretization. Section 3 establishes the discrete energy stability theory, including Hall cancellation and unconditional L2L^{2} stability, and discusses a formal higher-order HhsH_{h}^{s} estimate. Section 4 describes the Fourier realization of GhG_{h}, the integrating-factor treatment of Λα\Lambda^{\alpha}, and the spectral Hodge projection. Section 5 presents the numerical experiments. Appendix A introduces the BDF2 modified-energy stability theorem and its numerical verification.

2 Algorithm Description

This section develops the spatial and temporal discretization of the component system (2). We first introduce a C0C^{0} linear finite element space together with the gradient recovery operator that makes the second-order discrete Hall terms computable, then assemble the associated discrete Hall and current operators, and finally present the semi-implicit time discretization. The construction keeps the lowest-order Hall cancellation exact at the discrete level, which is the structural property exploited in the stability analysis of Section 3.

2.1 Spatial discretization and the recovery operator

Let 𝒯h\mathcal{T}_{h} be a shape-regular triangulation of Ω=[0,2​π]2\Omega=[0,2\pi]^{2} with mesh size hh. Define the C0C^{0} linear finite element space

Vh={vh∈𝒫1​(Ω,𝒯h):vh​ continuous at all ​p∈𝒩h},V_{h}=\{v_{h}\in\mathcal{P}_{1}(\Omega;\mathcal{T}_{h}):v_{h}\text{ continuous at all }p\in\mathcal{N}_{h}\},

where 𝒩h\mathcal{N}_{h} is the set of nodes (vertices) of 𝒯h\mathcal{T}_{h}. VhperV_{h}^{\mathrm{per}} denotes the subset of VhV_{h} with periodic boundary condition. For each vh∈Vhv_{h}\in V_{h}, let ℰh\mathcal{E}_{h} denote the sets of all edges, and let mem_{e} and 𝒦e\mathcal{K}_{e} denote the midpoint and the union of the two triangles sharing edge ee. Associate a Morley finite element function wh∈Mhw_{h}\in M_{h} by

wh(p)=vh(p)∀p∈𝒩h,∂wh∂𝒏e(me)=𝒏e⋅1|𝒦e|∫𝒦e∇vhdx∀e∈ℰh,w_{h}(p)=v_{h}(p)\;\forall\,p\in\mathcal{N}_{h},\qquad\frac{\partial w_{h}}{\partial\bm{n}_{e}}(m_{e})=\bm{n}_{e}\cdot\frac{1}{|\mathcal{K}_{e}|}\int_{\mathcal{K}_{e}}\nabla v_{h}\,dx\;\forall\,e\in\mathcal{E}_{h}, (4)

where 𝒏e\bm{n}_{e} is the unit normal to ee.

The gradient recovery operator Gh:Vh→𝒫1​(Ω,𝒯h)2G_{h}:V_{h}\to\mathcal{P}_{1}(\Omega;\mathcal{T}_{h})^{2} is defined by

Gh​vh|T=∇wh|T,for allT∈𝒯h.G_{h}v_{h}|_{T}=\nabla w_{h}|_{T},\quad\text{for all}\quad T\in\mathcal{T}_{h}.

We introduce GhG_{h} here on a general shape-regular triangulation; on the uniform periodic grid used in our computations it admits an explicit Fourier realization, derived in Section 4. The key property of GhG_{h} is captured in the following lemma.

Lemma 1 (Lemma 3.3 of [5]).

For any vh∈Vhv_{h}\in V_{h}, Gh​vh∈VhCR×VhCRG_{h}v_{h}\in V_{h}^{\mathrm{CR}}\times V_{h}^{\mathrm{CR}}, and

Gh​vh​(me)=1|𝒦e|​∫𝒦e∇vh​𝑑x∀e∈ℰh.G_{h}v_{h}(m_{e})=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{K}_{e}|}\int_{\mathcal{K}_{e}}\nabla v_{h}\,dx\qquad\forall\,e\in\mathcal{E}_{h}. (5)

This formula makes GhG_{h} cheap to compute (one patch average per edge) and avoids assembling Morley basis functions in practice. The stability equivalence ‖∇vh‖L2​(Ω)≲‖Gh​vh‖L2​(Ω)\left\|\nabla v_{h}\right\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)}\lesssim\left\|G_{h}v_{h}\right\|_{L^{2}(\Omega)} (Lemma 3.7 of [5]) and the discrete Poincaré inequality ‖∇vh‖L2≲‖D​Gh​vh‖L2​(𝒯h)\left\|\nabla v_{h}\right\|_{L^{2}}\lesssim\left\|DG_{h}v_{h}\right\|_{L^{2}(\mathcal{T}_{h})} hold on shape-regular meshes without uniformity assumptions.

Figure 1 illustrates the two geometric objects underlying the definition of GhG_{h}. Panel (a) shows the diamond-shaped patch 𝒦e=T1∪T2\mathcal{K}_{e}=T_{1}\cup T_{2} formed by the two triangles sharing interior edge ee: the midpoint mem_{e} lies on ee, the outward unit normal 𝒏e\bm{n}_{e} points from T2T_{2} into T1T_{1}, and the patch-average formula (5) assigns to mem_{e} the area-weighted mean of ∇vh\nabla v_{h} over the patch. Panel (b) shows a single triangle TT with edge midpoints me1,me2,me3m_{e_{1}},m_{e_{2}},m_{e_{3}} (squares); Gh​vhG_{h}v_{h} is a piecewise-linear vector field determined by its values at these midpoints, which is precisely the definition of the Crouzeix–Raviart space VhCR×VhCRV_{h}^{\mathrm{CR}}\times V_{h}^{\mathrm{CR}}.

2.2 Discrete operators

In the 2.52.5D setting the discrete solution is 𝑩h=(Bx,h,By,h,Bz,h)∈(Vhper)3\bm{B}_{h}=(B_{x,h},\,B_{y,h},\,B_{z,h})\in(V_{h}^{\mathrm{per}})^{3}. The in-plane pair (Bx,h,By,h)(B_{x,h},B_{y,h}) satisfies the divergence-free constraint ∇⋅x​y𝑩h=0\nabla\cdot_{xy}\bm{B}_{h}=0, while Bz,hB_{z,h} is a free scalar field.

1. Discrete in-plane curl

Jh|T=(Gh​By,h⋅𝒆x−Gh​Bx,h⋅𝒆y)|T,T∈𝒯h,J_{h}\big|_{T}\;=\;\bigl(G_{h}B_{y,h}\cdot\bm{e}_{x}-G_{h}B_{x,h}\cdot\bm{e}_{y}\bigr)\big|_{T},\qquad T\in\mathcal{T}_{h},

giving a piecewise-constant scalar Jh=∂x,hBy,h−∂y,hBx,hJ_{h}=\partial_{x,h}B_{y,h}-\partial_{y,h}B_{x,h} (the zz-component of ∇×h𝑩h\nabla\times_{h}\bm{B}_{h}).

2. Discrete Hall nonlinearity

Expanding ∇×((∇×𝑩)×𝑩)\nabla\times\bigl((\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}\bigr) component-by-component under ∂z=0\partial_{z}=0 separates the three equations as follows.

  • •

    In-plane (i=x,yi=x,y): the Hall force is ±∂i(𝑩⋅∇Bz)\pm\partial_{i}\bigl(\bm{B}\cdot\nabla B_{z}\bigr), treated semi-implicitly:

    𝒩hx​y​[𝑩hn,Bz,hn+1]x\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{h}^{xy}[\bm{B}_{h}^{n},B_{z,h}^{n+1}]_{x} =∂y,h(𝑩hn⋅Gh​Bz,hn+1),\displaystyle=\partial_{y,h}\bigl(\bm{B}_{h}^{n}\cdot G_{h}B_{z,h}^{n+1}\bigr), (6)
    𝒩hx​y​[𝑩hn,Bz,hn+1]y\displaystyle\mathcal{N}_{h}^{xy}[\bm{B}_{h}^{n},B_{z,h}^{n+1}]_{y} =−∂x,h(𝑩hn⋅GhBz,hn+1).\displaystyle=-\partial_{x,h}\bigl(\bm{B}_{h}^{n}\cdot G_{h}B_{z,h}^{n+1}\bigr).
  • •

    Out-of-plane (i=zi=z): the Hall force is 𝑩⋅∇J\bm{B}\cdot\nabla J, treated semi-implicitly:

    𝒩hz​[𝑩hn,𝑩hn+1]=𝑩hn⋅Gh​Jhn+1,Jhn+1=∂x,hBy,hn+1−∂y,hBx,hn+1.\mathcal{N}_{h}^{z}[\bm{B}_{h}^{n},\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1}]=\bm{B}_{h}^{n}\cdot G_{h}J_{h}^{n+1},\qquad J_{h}^{n+1}=\partial_{x,h}B_{y,h}^{n+1}-\partial_{y,h}B_{x,h}^{n+1}. (7)

Treating one factor of 𝑩\bm{B} explicitly linearizes each Hall term and reduces the problem to three coupled second-order linear systems in 𝑩hn+1\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1}.

3. Discrete fractional Laplacian

On the uniform periodic grid the fractional Laplacian Λα=(−Δ)α/2\Lambda^{\alpha}=(-\Delta)^{\alpha/2} is applied exactly in Fourier space (e.g., [30]):

(Λα​fh)^kx,ky=|kx2+ky2|α/2​f^kx,ky.\widehat{(\Lambda^{\alpha}f_{h})}_{k_{x},k_{y}}=|k_{x}^{2}+k_{y}^{2}|^{\alpha/2}\,\hat{f}_{k_{x},k_{y}}. (8)

This is exact for any α>0\alpha>0 and avoids the O⁡(h2)O(h^{2}) stencil error of the standard five-point approximation.

4. Edge-penalty bilinear form

To control jumps of the recovered gradient across edges, define (following [5, Eq. (4.4)])

bh​(uh,vh)=∑e∈ℰhhe−1​(⟦Gh​uh⟧,⟦Gh​vh⟧)L2​(e),b_{h}(u_{h},v_{h})=\sum_{e\in\mathcal{E}_{h}}h_{e}^{-1}\bigl(\llbracket G_{h}u_{h}\rrbracket,\llbracket G_{h}v_{h}\rrbracket\bigr)_{L^{2}(e)}, (9)

where ⟦⋅⟧\llbracket\cdot\rrbracket denotes the jump across ee.

Remark 2.

In contrast to the stabilization term in [5], the boundary penalty term is omitted here because periodic boundary conditions allow every edge to be treated as an interior edge.

2.3 Time discretization

Given 𝑩hn∈(Vhper)3\bm{B}_{h}^{n}\in(V_{h}^{\mathrm{per}})^{3}, find 𝑩hn+1∈(Vhper)3\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1}\in(V_{h}^{\mathrm{per}})^{3} such that for all (ϕx,ϕy,ϕz)∈(Vhper)3(\phi_{x},\phi_{y},\phi_{z})\in(V_{h}^{\mathrm{per}})^{3}:

1τ​(Bx,hn+1−Bx,hn,ϕx)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\tau}\bigl(B_{x,h}^{n+1}-B_{x,h}^{n},\phi_{x}\bigr) +(𝒩hx​y​[𝑩hn,Bz,hn+1]x,ϕx)+(Λhα​Bx,hn+1,ϕx)+σ​bh​(Bx,hn+1,ϕx)=0,\displaystyle+\bigl(\mathcal{N}_{h}^{xy}[\bm{B}_{h}^{n},B_{z,h}^{n+1}]_{x},\phi_{x}\bigr)+\bigl(\Lambda_{h}^{\alpha}B_{x,h}^{n+1},\phi_{x}\bigr)+\sigma\,b_{h}(B_{x,h}^{n+1},\phi_{x})=0, (10)
1τ​(By,hn+1−By,hn,ϕy)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\tau}\bigl(B_{y,h}^{n+1}-B_{y,h}^{n},\phi_{y}\bigr) +(𝒩hx​y​[𝑩hn,Bz,hn+1]y,ϕy)+(Λhα​By,hn+1,ϕy)+σ​bh​(By,hn+1,ϕy)=0,\displaystyle+\bigl(\mathcal{N}_{h}^{xy}[\bm{B}_{h}^{n},B_{z,h}^{n+1}]_{y},\phi_{y}\bigr)+\bigl(\Lambda_{h}^{\alpha}B_{y,h}^{n+1},\phi_{y}\bigr)+\sigma\,b_{h}(B_{y,h}^{n+1},\phi_{y})=0, (11)
1τ​(Bz,hn+1−Bz,hn,ϕz)\displaystyle\frac{1}{\tau}\bigl(B_{z,h}^{n+1}-B_{z,h}^{n},\phi_{z}\bigr) +(𝒩hz​[𝑩hn,𝑩hn+1],ϕz)+(Λhα​Bz,hn+1,ϕz)+σ​bh​(Bz,hn+1,ϕz)=0,\displaystyle+\bigl(\mathcal{N}_{h}^{z}[\bm{B}_{h}^{n},\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1}],\phi_{z}\bigr)+\bigl(\Lambda_{h}^{\alpha}B_{z,h}^{n+1},\phi_{z}\bigr)+\sigma\,b_{h}(B_{z,h}^{n+1},\phi_{z})=0, (12)

followed by the in-plane divergence-free projection (e.g., [28])

(Bx,hn+1,By,hn+1)←Phdiv​(Bx,hn+1,By,hn+1).\bigl(B_{x,h}^{n+1},B_{y,h}^{n+1}\bigr)\leftarrow P_{h}^{\mathrm{div}}\bigl(B_{x,h}^{n+1},B_{y,h}^{n+1}\bigr).

The semi-implicit formulation leads to coupled linear subproblems at each step: the in-plane pair (Bx,By)(B_{x},B_{y}) is driven by ∇Bzn+1\nabla B_{z}^{n+1} through (10)–(11), and BzB_{z} is driven by Jn+1J^{n+1} of (Bxn+1,Byn+1)(B_{x}^{n+1},B_{y}^{n+1}) through (12). In the implementation of Section 4, we use an integrating-factor variant in which all Hall forces are evaluated explicitly at time level nn, replacing the coupled linear solve by three independent Fourier updates. The semi-implicit coupled system (10)–(12) is the structure-preserving model underlying the stability analysis of Section 3; it is not solved directly in our experiments, which instead use the explicit-Hall integrating-factor implementation of Section 4.

Figure 2 summarizes the time-stepping loop, combining the recovery-based Hall evaluation, the integrating-factor update, and the spectral Hodge projection.

3 Stability analysis

This section presents the energy mechanism behind the scheme. The argument follows the dyadic energy method of [4], adapted to the periodic discrete operators used here. The essential point is that the Hall term must be discretized in a form that preserves the skew-symmetry of ∇×((∇×𝑩)×𝑩)\nabla\times((\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}). In the continuum, several componentwise forms are equivalent by the product rule and by ∇⋅𝑩=0\nabla\cdot\bm{B}=0. At the discrete level these identities are no longer automatic. For the stability proof we therefore use the curl–cross-product form below.

Let (⋅,⋅)h\left(\cdot,\cdot\right)_{h} denote the periodic grid inner product and assume that Dx,DyD_{x},D_{y} are periodic summation-by-parts operators,

(Dx​f,g)h=−(f,Dx​g)h,(Dy​f,g)h=−(f,Dy​g)h.\left(D_{x}f,g\right)_{h}=-\left(f,D_{x}g\right)_{h},\qquad\left(D_{y}f,g\right)_{h}=-\left(f,D_{y}g\right)_{h}. (13)

On the uniform periodic grid this is satisfied by the Fourier realization of GhG_{h}, whose symbols are purely imaginary and odd. Define the discrete 2.52.5D curl by

Ch​𝑩h:=(Dy​Bz,h,−Dx​Bz,h,Dx​By,h−Dy​Bx,h).C_{h}\bm{B}_{h}:=\bigl(D_{y}B_{z,h},\,-D_{x}B_{z,h},\,D_{x}B_{y,h}-D_{y}B_{x,h}\bigr). (14)

Then (13) implies the discrete curl identity

(Ch​𝑼h,𝑽h)h=(𝑼h,Ch​𝑽h)h,\left(C_{h}\bm{U}_{h},\bm{V}_{h}\right)_{h}=\left(\bm{U}_{h},C_{h}\bm{V}_{h}\right)_{h}, (15)

which is the periodic analogue of integration by parts for the curl operator.

For 𝑼h,𝑽h∈(Vhper)3\bm{U}_{h},\bm{V}_{h}\in(V_{h}^{\mathrm{per}})^{3}, define the linearized Hall operator

ℋh​(𝑼h,𝑽h):=Ch​((Ch​𝑼h)×𝑽h),\mathcal{H}_{h}(\bm{U}_{h};\bm{V}_{h}):=C_{h}\bigl((C_{h}\bm{U}_{h})\times\bm{V}_{h}\bigr), (16)

where 𝑼h\bm{U}_{h} is the implicit argument and 𝑽h\bm{V}_{h} is the frozen explicit field. This is the discrete counterpart of ∇×((∇×𝑩)×𝑩)\nabla\times((\nabla\times\bm{B})\times\bm{B}).

Remark 3.

On the uniform periodic grid the blocks Δqh\Delta_{q}^{h} satisfy the same Bernstein and almost-orthogonality properties as their continuous counterparts, so the continuous Chae–Wan–Wu paraproduct estimate ([4]) is expected to transfer to the discrete commutator with constants uniform in hh, giving

Remark 8.

Proposition 7 relies on the discrete paraproduct transfer used in the proof of Lemma 6, which we adopt formally by analogy with the continuous theory rather than prove through a discrete Littlewood–Paley calculus. It is therefore best read as a formal discrete analogue of the Chae–Wan–Wu estimate, demonstrating that the discretization respects the same Hall cancellation mechanism at higher regularity. The unconditional L2L^{2} stability of Theorem 5, by contrast, is fully rigorous and independent of this transfer.

Remark 9.

The Chae–Wan–Wu cancellation reduces the Hall contribution to a commutator that costs only one half derivative above the HhsH_{h}^{s} energy level, namely Hhs+1/2H_{h}^{s+1/2}. The dissipation generated by Λhα=(−Δh)α/2\Lambda_{h}^{\alpha}=(-\Delta_{h})^{\alpha/2} controls Hhs+α/2H_{h}^{s+\alpha/2}. Therefore the interpolation step (31) requires s+1/2<s+α/2s+1/2<s+\alpha/2, which is exactly α>1\alpha>1. In the notation of [4], the diffusion is written as (−Δ)α(-\Delta)^{\alpha}, so the corresponding condition is α>1/2\alpha>1/2.

Remark 10.

The integrating-factor Euler update

𝑩^𝒌n+1=e−|𝒌|α​τ​(𝑩^𝒌n−τ​ℋ⁡[𝑩n]^𝒌)\widehat{\bm{B}}^{n+1}_{\bm{k}}=e^{-|\bm{k}|^{\alpha}\tau}\left(\widehat{\bm{B}}^{n}_{\bm{k}}-\tau\widehat{\mathcal{H}[\bm{B}^{n}]}_{\bm{k}}\right)

is unconditionally stable for the fractional diffusion substep, but it does not inherit the exact nonlinear energy identity of Theorem 5. Even if (ℋ⁡[𝐁hn],𝐁hn)h=0\left(\mathcal{H}[\bm{B}_{h}^{n}],\bm{B}_{h}^{n}\right)_{h}=0, the explicit Hall update gives

‖𝑩hn−τ​ℋ​[𝑩hn]‖0,h2=‖𝑩hn‖0,h2+τ2​‖ℋ⁡[𝑩hn]‖0,h2.\left\|\bm{B}_{h}^{n}-\tau\mathcal{H}[\bm{B}_{h}^{n}]\right\|_{0,h}^{2}=\left\|\bm{B}_{h}^{n}\right\|_{0,h}^{2}+\tau^{2}\left\|\mathcal{H}[\bm{B}_{h}^{n}]\right\|_{0,h}^{2}.

Thus the diffusion part is unconditional, whereas the fully explicit Hall part remains subject to a Hall CFL condition. The unconditional nonlinear energy estimate is a property of the semi-implicit curl-form discretization (18). A second-order BDF2 variant of the scheme, which satisfies an analogous modified-energy stability theorem, is described in Appendix A.

4 Implementation on the Uniform Periodic Grid

All computations are carried out on the uniform N×NN\times N periodic grid on Ω=[0,2​π]2\Omega=[0,2\pi]^{2} with grid spacing h=2​π/Nh=2\pi/N. On this grid the recovery operators admit an exact Fourier realization, so all differential operators are evaluated via FFTs. While the analysis of Section 3 is carried out for the semi-implicit curl-form discretization (18), all numerical experiments in Section 5 use the explicit-Hall integrating-factor implementation described below. The two schemes are based on the same Hall operator and differential identities, but the explicit-Hall implementation is unconditionally stable only for the fractional-diffusion substep and does not inherit the exact nonlinear energy identity of Theorem 5 (see Remark 10). We use the explicit-Hall implementation in the experiments because it is computationally simpler on the periodic grid, reducing each step to a few FFTs, while the semi-implicit formulation is what exposes the discrete Hall cancellation and supplies the stability mechanism.

Spectral realization of the recovery gradient GhG_{h}

On the uniform N×NN\times N Cartesian grid, every interior edge patch 𝒦e\mathcal{K}_{e} consists of two right triangles whose union is an h×hh\times h square. In this geometry the patch average of ∇vh\nabla v_{h} over 𝒦e\mathcal{K}_{e} reduces to a fixed linear combination of nodal values. Summing over all contributing patches yields the nine-point stencil

(Gh​f)i,jx=14​h​[(fi+1,j−fi−1,j)+12​(fi+1,j+1−fi−1,j+1)+12​(fi+1,j−1−fi−1,j−1)],(G_{h}f)^{x}_{i,j}=\frac{1}{4h}\Bigl[\bigl(f_{i+1,j}-f_{i-1,j}\bigr)+\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(f_{i+1,j+1}-f_{i-1,j+1}\bigr)+\tfrac{1}{2}\bigl(f_{i+1,j-1}-f_{i-1,j-1}\bigr)\Bigr], (32)

with the yy-component given by symmetry. This is a separable convolution: a central difference in xx followed by the averaging filter 14​[δj−1+2​δj+δj+1]\tfrac{1}{4}[\delta_{j-1}+2\delta_{j}+\delta_{j+1}] in yy.

Taking the 2D DFT with integer wavenumbers (kx,ky)∈{−N/2+1,…,N/2}2(k_{x},k_{y})\in\{-N/2+1,\ldots,N/2\}^{2}, the Fourier symbol of GhG_{h} is

(Gh​f)x^kx,ky=σx(kx,ky)f^kx,ky,σx(kx,ky)=−i​sin⁡(kx​h)h⋅1+cos⁡(ky​h)2.\widehat{(G_{h}f)^{x}}_{k_{x},k_{y}}=\sigma^{x}(k_{x},k_{y})\,\hat{f}_{k_{x},k_{y}},\qquad\sigma^{x}(k_{x},k_{y})=-\frac{i\sin(k_{x}h)}{h}\cdot\frac{1+\cos(k_{y}h)}{2}. (33)
Remark 11 (Accuracy and aliasing suppression).

The exact spectral xx-derivative has symbol i​kxik_{x}. The stencil symbol satisfies

σx​(kx,ky)=−i​kx​[1−(kx​h)26+O⁡((kx​h)4)]​[1−(ky​h)24+O⁡((ky​h)4)],\sigma^{x}(k_{x},k_{y})=-ik_{x}\Bigl[1-\tfrac{(k_{x}h)^{2}}{6}+O((k_{x}h)^{4})\Bigr]\Bigl[1-\tfrac{(k_{y}h)^{2}}{4}+O((k_{y}h)^{4})\Bigr],

so σx=−i​kx+O⁡((k​h)2)\sigma^{x}=-ik_{x}+O((kh)^{2}) for resolved modes. At the Nyquist frequency ky=N/2k_{y}=N/2, the averaging factor (1+cos⁡(π))/2=0(1+\cos(\pi))/2=0 damps the corresponding near-Nyquist modes, providing a mild built-in filtering effect; this is not, however, a full de-aliasing rule for nonlinear products. In the code, (32) is applied via numpy.fft.fft2/ifft2, which is bit-for-bit equivalent to direct stencil application but generalizes trivially to any Fourier-diagonal operator.

Fractional Laplacian via integrating factor

On the uniform periodic grid, Λα\Lambda^{\alpha} is applied exactly in Fourier space by (8). The integrating-factor update

B^𝒌n+1=e−|𝒌|α​τ​(B^𝒌n−τ​ℋ⁡[𝑩n]^𝒌),\hat{B}^{n+1}_{\bm{k}}=e^{-|\bm{k}|^{\alpha}\tau}\bigl(\hat{B}^{n}_{\bm{k}}-\tau\,\widehat{\mathcal{H}[\bm{B}^{n}]}_{\bm{k}}\bigr), (34)

where ℋ\mathcal{H} denotes the explicit Hall term, handles dissipation exactly regardless of τ\tau and hh. The remaining practical time-step restriction is the hyperbolic Hall CFL τ≲h/max⁡|𝑩|\tau\lesssim h/\max|\bm{B}|.

Remark 12 (Unconditional stability of the IF method).

For any α>0\alpha>0 and τ,h>0\tau,h>0, the integrating factor e−|𝐤|α​τ∈(0,1]e^{-|\bm{k}|^{\alpha}\tau}\in(0,1] for all 𝐤\bm{k}. This means the diffusion step in (34) is unconditionally stable: regardless of how large τ\tau is, no Fourier mode grows from the dissipation. In contrast, a fully explicit treatment of the fractional diffusion would require a parabolic time-step restriction τ≲hα/C\tau\lesssim h^{\alpha}/C.

Divergence-free projection

After the Hall update, the in-plane components acquire a spurious divergence of order O⁡(τ​h)O(\tau h). This is corrected by a spectral Hodge projection: solve Δ​ϕ=∇⋅𝑩\Delta\phi=\nabla\cdot\bm{B} in Fourier space,

ϕ^𝒌=−(∇⋅𝑩)^𝒌|𝒌|2,|𝒌|≠0,\hat{\phi}_{\bm{k}}=-\frac{\widehat{(\nabla\cdot\bm{B})}_{\bm{k}}}{|\bm{k}|^{2}},\quad|\bm{k}|\neq 0,

and set 𝑩←𝑩−∇ϕ\bm{B}\leftarrow\bm{B}-\nabla\phi. This reduces max⁡|∇⋅𝑩h|\max|\nabla\cdot\bm{B}_{h}| to the round-off floor (10−1610^{-16}–10−1310^{-13}, scaling with the field amplitude and its gradients) and costs two forward and two inverse FFTs. The out-of-plane component BzB_{z} requires no projection.

Coupling summary

The in-plane pair (Bx,By)(B_{x},B_{y}) is forced by ∇Bz\nabla B_{z} through the Hall terms (6); BzB_{z} is forced by the in-plane current J=∂xBy−∂yBxJ=\partial_{x}B_{y}-\partial_{y}B_{x} through (7). In the explicit-Hall implementation, all three components use only the time-nn state in the Hall force evaluation, so the coupling within a step is one-directional. The complete update is:

  1. (i)

    Evaluate Hall forces (Hxn,Hyn,Hzn)(H_{x}^{n},H_{y}^{n},H_{z}^{n}) using (33).

  2. (ii)

    Apply integrating-factor step (34): unconditionally stable.

  3. (iii)

    Project (Bxn+1,Byn+1)(B_{x}^{n+1},B_{y}^{n+1}) via spectral Hodge: divergence to round-off.

5 Numerical Examples

All experiments use the periodic domain Ω=[0,2​π]2\Omega=[0,2\pi]^{2} on a uniform N=128N=128 grid (h=2​π/128≈0.049h=2\pi/128\approx 0.049) with time step τ=0.001\tau=0.001 and the integrating-factor Euler scheme of Section 4. The Hall CFL condition τ≲h/max⁡|𝑩|\tau\lesssim h/\max|\bm{B}| is comfortably satisfied for all field amplitudes considered. The spectral Hodge projection drives max⁡|∇⋅𝑩h|\max|\nabla\cdot\bm{B}_{h}| to the round-off floor (10−1610^{-16}–10−1310^{-13} depending on the field amplitude) at every step; see Tables 1 and 2.

We first establish the spatial accuracy of the scheme through a convergence study, then present three qualitatively distinct benchmark initial conditions: Example 1 subjects a sharp shear layer to mild Hall forcing and tests stable evolution of a sharp-gradient configuration; Example 2 balances Hall and dissipation to exhibit island merging; and Example 3 provides a controlled verification against an analytically computable multi-mode decay formula.

Spatial convergence

Table 1 reports L2L^{2} and H1H^{1} errors for the three fractional exponents against a fine reference solution. We use the smooth Orszag–Tang type initial condition,

Bx\displaystyle B_{x} =0.3​(−sin⁡y+0.1​cos⁡(2​x)​cos⁡y),\displaystyle=0.3\bigl(-\sin y+0.1\cos(2x)\cos y\bigr),
By\displaystyle B_{y} =0.3​(sin⁡x+0.1​sin⁡x​sin⁡(2​y)),\displaystyle=0.3\bigl(\sin x+0.1\sin x\,\sin(2y)\bigr),
Bz\displaystyle B_{z} =0.15​(cos⁡x+cos⁡y),\displaystyle=0.15(\cos x+\cos y),

followed by the spectral Hodge projection of the in-plane components. The time step τ\tau is held fixed across all grid resolutions (and is also used for the reference solution). This prevents temporal errors from contaminating the comparison and isolates the observed spatial convergence, without requiring τ\tau to scale with hh. The reference solution is computed on a substantially finer grid, using N=512N=512 for α=1.5\alpha=1.5 and 2.02.0, and N=384N=384 for α=1.2\alpha=1.2. Since weaker dissipation requires a smaller time step to maintain stability, using N=384N=384 for α=1.2\alpha=1.2 avoids the more restrictive time-step requirement associated with N=512N=512.

The L2L^{2} rate increases from approximately 1.861.86 (N=16→32N=16\to 32) to approximately 2.12.1 (N=64→128N=64\to 128), and the H1H^{1} rate similarly approaches approximately 2.12.1, consistent with the second-order accuracy of GhG_{h} on the uniform periodic grid. The rates are consistent across all values of α\alpha, confirming that they reflect the spatial accuracy of GhG_{h} rather than α\alpha-dependent dynamics. The divergence error remains near round-off (10−1610^{-16}–10−1510^{-15}) throughout, validating the spectral Hodge projection.

Example 1. Kelvin–Helmholtz shear layer (α=1.2\alpha=1.2).

We choose the following initial condition,

Bx=−1+tanh⁡(y−π/20.5)−tanh⁡(y−3​π/20.5)+0.1​sin⁡x​cos⁡2​y,\displaystyle B_{x}=-1+\tanh\!\Bigl(\frac{y-\pi/2}{0.5}\Bigr)-\tanh\!\Bigl(\frac{y-3\pi/2}{0.5}\Bigr)+0.1\sin x\cos 2y, (35)
By=0.1​cos⁡2​x​sin⁡y+0.05​sin⁡3​x,\displaystyle B_{y}=0.1\cos 2x\sin y+0.05\sin 3x,
Bz=0.5​sin⁡x​sin⁡y+0.3​cos⁡2​x​cos⁡y,\displaystyle B_{z}=0.5\sin x\sin y+0.3\cos 2x\cos y,

followed by the spectral Hodge projection of the in-plane components. The two oppositely-signed interfaces at y=π/2y=\pi/2 and y=3​π/2y=3\pi/2, each of width ≈0.5\approx 0.5, make BxB_{x} exactly periodic in yy; this is essential on the spectral grid, since a single interface would leave a jump across the seam y=0≡2​πy=0\equiv 2\pi that the periodic derivative would render as a spurious boundary current dominating the physical layers. The double-interface profile generates two genuine shear layers with max⁡|Jh|≈2.3\max|J_{h}|\approx 2.3 at t=0t=0 (post-projection energy E0≈0.77E_{0}\approx 0.77). Multi-mode perturbations in ByB_{y} and the non-trivial BzB_{z} break translational symmetry and seed the Hall coupling.

Physical regime

With α=1.2\alpha=1.2 the fractional operator damps large wavenumbers only weakly. For the dominant modes at |k|∼1|k|\sim 1 the dissipation rate |k|α=1|k|^{\alpha}=1 is exceeded by the Hall forcing |𝑩|​|∇J|≈3|\bm{B}||\nabla J|\approx 3, so this is a mildly Hall-dominated test: the Hall term deforms the shear layers and couples them to BzB_{z} without overwhelming the dissipation [3].

Dynamics

Figure 3 traces the evolution at t∈{0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.45}t\in\{0,\,0.10,\,0.25,\,0.45\}. At t=0t=0 the current density JhJ_{h} shows two coherent horizontal bands of opposite sign at y=π/2y=\pi/2 and y=3​π/2y=3\pi/2. By t=0.10t=0.10 the Hall coupling to BzB_{z} has imposed a gentle in-plane undulation on these bands; max⁡|Jh|\max|J_{h}| has decreased from 2.322.32 to 1.931.93 and the energy from E0≈0.77E_{0}\approx 0.77 to ≈0.61\approx 0.61. By t=0.25t=0.25 the bands carry a clear wavy modulation with max⁡|Jh|=1.51\max|J_{h}|=1.51 (E/E0=0.57E/E_{0}=0.57), and by t=0.45t=0.45 they remain coherent but visibly rippled, with max⁡|Jh|=1.06\max|J_{h}|=1.06 (E/E0=0.37E/E_{0}=0.37). The normalized spatial correlation between JhJ_{h} at t=0t=0 and t=0.45t=0.45 is 0.890.89: the Hall term reshapes the layers without destroying them, so the evolution is a stable, mildly Hall-perturbed decay. This is the expected behavior for smooth, moderate-amplitude shear data in the mildly Hall-dominated regime, and serves as a stress test of the scheme on a sharp-gradient configuration.

Effect of α\alpha

Figure 4 and Table 2 show the sensitivity to the fractional exponent over t∈[0,0.2]t\in[0,0.2]. The normalized energy E⁡(T)/E0E(T)/E_{0} equals 0.6370.637, 0.6280.628, and 0.6160.616 for α=1.2\alpha=1.2, 1.51.5, and 2.02.0: a spread of only about 3%3\%, because the energy is dominated by large-scale modes at |k|∼1|k|\sim 1 where |k|α|k|^{\alpha} varies little between exponents. The enstrophy Ω⁡(T)/Ω0\Omega(T)/\Omega_{0} equals 0.5900.590, 0.5600.560, and 0.5270.527: a relative spread of about 11%11\%. The asymmetry — a small energy difference but a larger enstrophy difference — is the fingerprint of the fractional Laplacian acting preferentially at high wavenumbers, where the k2k^{2}-weighted enstrophy places more of its mass.

Example 2. Magnetic island merging (α=1.5\alpha=1.5).

We choose the following initial condition,

Bx\displaystyle B_{x} =2​(sin⁡2​x​cos⁡y+0.5​sin⁡x​cos⁡2​y+0.3​sin⁡3​x​cos⁡y),\displaystyle=2\bigl(\sin 2x\cos y+0.5\sin x\cos 2y+0.3\sin 3x\cos y\bigr), (36)
By\displaystyle B_{y} =−2​(cos⁡2​x​sin⁡y+0.5​cos⁡x​sin⁡2​y+0.3​cos⁡3​x​sin⁡y),\displaystyle=-2\bigl(\cos 2x\sin y+0.5\cos x\sin 2y+0.3\cos 3x\sin y\bigr),
Bz\displaystyle B_{z} =2​(cos⁡x​cos⁡y+0.4​cos⁡2​x+0.4​cos⁡2​y+0.2​cos⁡3​x​cos⁡y),\displaystyle=2\bigl(\cos x\cos y+0.4\cos 2x+0.4\cos 2y+0.2\cos 3x\cos y\bigr),

followed by the spectral Hodge projection of the in-plane components. The in-plane field is a superposition of Fourier modes at wavenumbers k=1,2,3k=1,2,3 that produce closed flux tubes (magnetic islands) of decreasing size; it is rendered divergence-free by the Hodge projection applied at initialization, which brings the raw energy (≈4.36\approx 4.36) down to the reported E0≈4.07E_{0}\approx 4.07, with max⁡|Jh|≈8.7\max|J_{h}|\approx 8.7. This configuration is the natural periodic analogue of the island coalescence problem studied in [25, 1, 12].

Physical motivation and regime

Magnetic island coalescence is a canonical driven-reconnection problem [25]: the attraction between same-helicity islands drives current-sheet formation between them. With α=1.5\alpha=1.5 the Hall/dissipation ratio for the dominant k=2k=2 modes is |𝑩|​|k|2/|k|α≈2.8|\bm{B}||k|^{2}/|k|^{\alpha}\approx 2.8, so the Hall term and the dissipation are in genuine competition, deforming the islands while smoothing fine scales.

Dynamics

Figure 5 traces the evolution at t∈{0, 0.10, 0.25, 0.40}t\in\{0,\,0.10,\,0.25,\,0.40\}. At t=0t=0 the JhJ_{h} field shows regular thin current filaments at the island boundaries. By t=0.10t=0.10 the Hall term has distorted the boundaries and generated fine-scale current concentrations; the smallest (k=3k=3) islands begin merging with neighbors. By t=0.25t=0.25 the k=3k=3 islands have been substantially absorbed, and the current pattern is dominated by elongated filaments between formerly distinct islands, showing structures consistent with Hall-dominated reconnection. By t=0.40t=0.40 the multi-island pattern has reorganized into two or three dominant flux-tube structures; the JhJ_{h} correlation between t=0t=0 and t=0.40t=0.40 is 0.510.51, indicating significant structural change while some memory of the initial configuration is retained.

Example 3. Helical initial data and verification (α=2.0\alpha=2.0).

We choose the following initial condition,

Bx\displaystyle B_{x} =sin⁡x​cos⁡y+0.5​cos⁡(2​x)​sin⁡y,\displaystyle=\sin x\cos y+0.5\cos(2x)\sin y, (37)
By\displaystyle B_{y} =−cos⁡x​sin⁡y+0.5​sin⁡x​cos⁡(2​y),\displaystyle=-\cos x\sin y+0.5\sin x\cos(2y),
Bz\displaystyle B_{z} =sin⁡x+sin⁡y.\displaystyle=\sin x+\sin y.

After the divergence-free projection, the initial energy of (37) is E0≈1.53E_{0}\approx 1.53. Under Λ2=−Δ\Lambda^{2}=-\Delta, the Fourier modes with |k|2=1|k|^{2}=1, 22, and 55 decay respectively as e−te^{-t}, e−2​te^{-2t}, and e−5​te^{-5t}, and account for approximately 65.6%65.6\%, 32.8%32.8\%, and 1.6%1.6\% of the total energy. These percentages are the post-projection energy split: the |k|2=5|k|^{2}=5 in-plane pair in (37) is not divergence-free, so the Hodge projection removes most of its energy and lowers E0E_{0} from its raw value ≈1.63\approx 1.63 to ≈1.53\approx 1.53. Since E⁡(t)=‖𝑩‖L22E(t)=\|\bm{B}\|_{L^{2}}^{2} is quadratic, the linearized energy follows

E⁡(t)E0=0.656​e−2​t+0.328​e−4​t+0.016​e−10​t+𝒪⁡(‖𝑩‖2).\frac{E(t)}{E_{0}}=0.656\,e^{-2t}+0.328\,e^{-4t}+0.016\,e^{-10t}+\mathcal{O}(\|\bm{B}\|^{2}). (38)

Verification

With α=2\alpha=2 the integrating factor is e−|k|2​τe^{-|k|^{2}\tau}, exact with no approximation. Any deviation from (38) measures the cumulative effect of the Hall nonlinearity. The Hall/dissipation ratio for Group B modes is |𝑩|​|k|2/|k|α=1⋅2/2=1|\bm{B}||k|^{2}/|k|^{\alpha}=1\cdot 2/2=1: Hall and dissipation are comparable, making this a mildly nonlinear verification test rather than a turbulence simulation.

Table 3 compares E⁡(t)/E0E(t)/E_{0} against (38) at six output times. The error is 0.60%0.60\% at t=0.25t=0.25, growing to 2.88%2.88\% at t=1.0t=1.0 and then saturating near 3%3\% for t≥1.0t\geq 1.0. The plateau indicates that the nonlinear correction is accumulated during the active Hall phase t∈[0,1]t\in[0,1] and then freezes as the field becomes too small for the Hall term to matter. A 3%3\% departure from the linearized formula at T=1T=1 confirms that the Hall term is present and active but sub-dominant, as expected for moderate-amplitude smooth initial data.

Energy and current histories

Figure 6 compares all three examples over t∈[0,0.6]t\in[0,0.6]. The left panel plots absolute energy E⁡(t)E(t) on a log scale. The three examples have initial amplitudes E0≈0.77E_{0}\approx 0.77 (KH shear), 4.074.07 (magnetic islands), and 1.531.53 (helical), and decay at rates determined jointly by α\alpha and spatial structure. The right panel plots max⁡|Jh​(t)|\max|J_{h}(t)|, a sensitive indicator of current-sheet intensity. The magnetic-island example carries the highest current density throughout, reflecting its larger field amplitude and the thin current filaments at the island boundaries; the helical example decays most smoothly, consistent with the linearized formula (38).

Appendix A Stability of a BDF2 variant

The energy framework of Section 3 extends to a second-order-in-time variant based on the Backward Differentiation Formula of order 2 (BDF2). The numerical experiments are based primarily on the integrating-factor Euler implementation; the results below provide mathematical support for future use of higher-order time stepping.

For problems where a larger time step is desirable, the energy framework extends naturally to the second-order Backward Differentiation Formula (BDF2) scheme. Given 𝑩hn\bm{B}_{h}^{n} and 𝑩hn−1\bm{B}_{h}^{n-1}, let 𝑩~hn:=2​𝑩hn−𝑩hn−1\widetilde{\bm{B}}_{h}^{n}:=2\bm{B}_{h}^{n}-\bm{B}_{h}^{n-1} be the second-order extrapolation. The BDF2 semi-implicit step is

3​𝑩hn+1,∗−4​𝑩hn+𝑩hn−12​τ+ℋh​(𝑩hn+1,∗,𝑩~hn)+Λhα​𝑩hn+1,∗+σ​Lb,h​𝑩hn+1,∗=0,\frac{3\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1,*}-4\bm{B}_{h}^{n}+\bm{B}_{h}^{n-1}}{2\tau}+\mathcal{H}_{h}(\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1,*};\widetilde{\bm{B}}_{h}^{n})+\Lambda_{h}^{\alpha}\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1,*}+\sigma L_{b,h}\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1,*}=0, (39)

followed by the Hodge projection 𝑩hn+1=Phdiv​𝑩hn+1,∗\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1}=P_{h}^{\mathrm{div}}\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1,*}.

Define the BDF2 modified magnetic energy

ℰhn:=12​(‖𝑩hn‖0,h2+‖2​𝑩hn−𝑩hn−1‖0,h2).\mathcal{E}_{h}^{n}:=\frac{1}{2}\Bigl(\left\|\bm{B}_{h}^{n}\right\|_{0,h}^{2}+\left\|2\bm{B}_{h}^{n}-\bm{B}_{h}^{n-1}\right\|_{0,h}^{2}\Bigr). (40)

The factor ‖2​𝑩hn−𝑩hn−1‖0,h2\left\|2\bm{B}_{h}^{n}-\bm{B}_{h}^{n-1}\right\|_{0,h}^{2} is the standard BDF2 correction term that makes the modified energy equivalent to ‖𝑩hn‖0,h2\left\|\bm{B}_{h}^{n}\right\|_{0,h}^{2} up to a constant factor.

Theorem 13 (BDF2 modified-energy stability).

Under the assumptions of Theorem 5, if 𝐁hn\bm{B}_{h}^{n} and 𝐁hn−1\bm{B}_{h}^{n-1} are in the range of PhdivP_{h}^{\mathrm{div}}, then every step of (39) satisfies

ℰhn+1,∗\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{h}^{n+1,*} +12​‖𝑩hn+1,∗−2​𝑩hn+𝑩hn−1‖0,h2+2​τ​‖Λhα/2​𝑩hn+1,∗‖0,h2\displaystyle+\frac{1}{2}\left\|\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1,*}-2\bm{B}_{h}^{n}+\bm{B}_{h}^{n-1}\right\|_{0,h}^{2}+2\tau\left\|\Lambda_{h}^{\alpha/2}\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1,*}\right\|_{0,h}^{2}
+2τσ∑i=x,y,zbh(Bi,hn+1,∗,Bi,hn+1,∗)=ℰhn,\displaystyle\quad+2\tau\sigma\sum_{i=x,y,z}b_{h}(B_{i,h}^{n+1,*},B_{i,h}^{n+1,*})=\mathcal{E}_{h}^{n}, (41)

where ℰhn+1,∗\mathcal{E}_{h}^{n+1,*} is defined with 𝐁hn+1,∗\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1,*} in place of 𝐁hn+1\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1}. Consequently,

ℰhn+1+2​τ​‖Λhα/2​𝑩hn+1,∗‖0,h2+2​τ​σ​∑i=x,y,zbh​(Bi,hn+1,∗,Bi,hn+1,∗)≤ℰhn.\mathcal{E}_{h}^{n+1}+2\tau\left\|\Lambda_{h}^{\alpha/2}\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1,*}\right\|_{0,h}^{2}+2\tau\sigma\sum_{i=x,y,z}b_{h}(B_{i,h}^{n+1,*},B_{i,h}^{n+1,*})\leq\mathcal{E}_{h}^{n}. (42)

Proof.

Take the inner product of (39) with 𝑩hn+1,∗\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1,*}. The Hall term vanishes by Lemma 4 (applied with the frozen field 𝑩~hn\widetilde{\bm{B}}_{h}^{n} in place of 𝑽h\bm{V}_{h}). The BDF2 time-difference identity

2​(3​a−4​b+c,a)h=‖a‖0,h2+‖2​a−b‖0,h2−‖b‖0,h2−‖2​b−c‖0,h2+‖a−2​b+c‖0,h2\displaystyle 2\left(3a-4b+c,a\right)_{h}=\left\|a\right\|_{0,h}^{2}+\left\|2a-b\right\|_{0,h}^{2}-\left\|b\right\|_{0,h}^{2}-\left\|2b-c\right\|_{0,h}^{2}+\left\|a-2b+c\right\|_{0,h}^{2}

with a=𝑩hn+1,∗a=\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1,*}, b=𝑩hnb=\bm{B}_{h}^{n}, c=𝑩hn−1c=\bm{B}_{h}^{n-1}, multiplied by 2​τ2\tau, gives (41). The projected estimate (42) follows because PhdivP_{h}^{\mathrm{div}} is orthogonal and 𝑩hn\bm{B}_{h}^{n} is already in its range, so ‖𝑩hn+1‖0,h≤‖𝑩hn+1,∗‖0,h\left\|\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1}\right\|_{0,h}\leq\left\|\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1,*}\right\|_{0,h} and ‖2​𝑩hn+1−𝑩hn‖0,h≤‖2​𝑩hn+1,∗−𝑩hn‖0,h\left\|2\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1}-\bm{B}_{h}^{n}\right\|_{0,h}\leq\left\|2\bm{B}_{h}^{n+1,*}-\bm{B}_{h}^{n}\right\|_{0,h}.

Remark 14 (Comparison of the two schemes).

Both the backward-Euler scheme (18) and the BDF2 scheme (39) are unconditionally stable in their respective energy norms, and both treat the Hall nonlinearity with a single frozen explicit factor, so both require the Hall CFL τ≲h/max⁡|𝐁h|\tau\lesssim h/\max|\bm{B}_{h}| for accuracy rather than stability. The backward-Euler scheme is first-order in time and simpler to start (no previous-step value required). The BDF2 scheme carries a larger stability constant and requires a warm-start Euler step, but its modified-energy identity (41) retains the same unconditional character. In the numerical experiments of Section 5 we use the integrating-factor Euler implementation as the primary scheme; Table 4 records the modified-energy behavior of the BDF2 variant for completeness.

Numerical verification

Table 4 verifies Theorem 13 numerically. For each of the three examples and each α∈{1.2,1.5,2.0}\alpha\in\{1.2,1.5,2.0\}, we run 200200 BDF2 steps on an N=32N=32 grid with τ=0.002\tau=0.002, and record the initial and final modified energy ℰhn\mathcal{E}_{h}^{n} defined in (40), together with the number of steps at which ℰhn\mathcal{E}_{h}^{n} increases (a violation of Theorem 13).

In every case the modified energy is strictly monotone throughout the run, confirming the theoretical estimate (42). The ratio ℰh200/ℰh0\mathcal{E}_{h}^{200}/\mathcal{E}_{h}^{0} reflects physical energy dissipation: faster fractional damping (larger α\alpha) leads to a smaller final-to-initial ratio.
